title: Acute Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: Recognition and Emergency Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Women in late pregnancy or the months after delivery with suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) presenting to the emergency department (ED), obstetric unit or medical ward: recognition, natriuretic peptide, electrocardiogram and echocardiography, acute heart failure care that is safe in pregnancy and lactation, bromocriptine with anticoagulation, delivery planning, referral to an intensive care unit (ICU) or tertiary centre, and follow-up. Uses the Heart Failure Association of the European Society of Cardiology (HFA/ESC) 2019 PPCM position statement and 2021 pregnancy cardiomyopathy statement, and product labels.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi PPCM guideline was found; a 2003 Saudi Medical Journal review was read but contains no recommendations used here.
The ESC 2018 guideline on cardiovascular disease in pregnancy, cited by both statements for the bromocriptine recommendation, was not opened.

Doses of oral heart failure drugs safe in pregnancy or lactation (beta-blockers, nitrates, hydralazine) are not given by these statements and are not listed; give them as advised by cardiology and obstetric pharmacy.
The enoxaparin prophylactic dose is from the product information; the statements specify only at least prophylactic anticoagulation.
Typical normal ranges for blood pressure, foetal heart rate and natriuretic peptides in pregnancy are not from these sources except the exclusion thresholds quoted.

pathophysiology.summary: PPCM is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 45% and no other cause (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Definition and epidemiology, p. 828). Oxidative stress cleaves prolactin into a cardiotoxic fragment, the target of bromocriptine (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Abstract). A genetic cause, often a titin truncating variant, is present in up to 20% (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Abstract). Pregnancy volume load and hormonal stress can unmask a pre-existing genetic or acquired cardiomyopathy (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Pathophysiology). Patients are especially sensitive to toxic effects of beta-adrenergic stimulation (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Section Acute heart failure, p. 833).

symptoms: Shortness of breath, fatigue, chest pain, cough and abdominal discomfort (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Section Clinical presentation, p. 829).
Leg oedema, which is common in normal pregnancy, so suspicion must be high (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Abstract).
physicalSigns: Signs of congestion: pulmonary crackles and oedema (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Tachycardia and hypotension in cardiogenic shock (HFA/ESC 2021, Figure 1).
Abnormal electrocardiogram, rarely normal at presentation (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 829).
redFlags: Cardiogenic shock or need for inotropes or vasopressors: early transfer to a centre with mechanical circulatory support; consider urgent caesarean delivery (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
LVEF below 25% or right ventricular involvement (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 838).
Intracardiac thrombus, systemic embolism or atrial fibrillation: therapeutic anticoagulation (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Section Drug therapy, p. 837).
Acute heart failure in pregnancy: immediate ICU referral with foetal assessment (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
precipitants: Multiparity and multiple pregnancy (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 828).
Family history and ethnicity (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 828).
Older maternal age, smoking, diabetes, malnutrition (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 828).
Prolonged tocolysis with beta-agonists (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 828).
Previous cardiotoxic cancer treatment (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Pathophysiology).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: BNP 100 pg/mL or more, NT-proBNP 300 pg/mL or more
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Mainly to rule out heart failure; not diagnostic of PPCM alone; levels stay normal in healthy pregnancy (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Section Biomarkers; HFA/ESC 2021, Section Natriuretic peptides).
ruleIn.normalValue: BNP below 100 pg/mL; NT-proBNP below 300 pg/mL

clinicalManagement.title: Suspect and test
actions: Keep a high index of suspicion for breathlessness, fatigue or oedema late in pregnancy or after delivery (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Abstract).
Do ECG and BNP; get echocardiography as soon as possible if either is abnormal (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, pp. 829 to 833; HFA/ESC 2021, Section Peripartum cardiomyopathy).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat acute heart failure
actions: Pregnant with acute heart failure: refer to ICU at once and assess the foetus (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Give loop diuretic for congestion, with foetal monitoring (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Nitrates are safe in pregnancy (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Avoid beta-adrenergic agonists such as dobutamine where possible; noradrenaline restores blood pressure (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 833).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate cardiogenic shock
actions: Transfer early to a tertiary centre able to provide mechanical circulatory support (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Consider urgent caesarean section regardless of gestation with mechanical support available (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).

clinicalManagement.title: Safe drugs and bromocriptine
actions: During pregnancy avoid angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Start and up-titrate beta-blockers with caution after stabilisation (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Postpartum, consider bromocriptine with at least prophylactic anticoagulation (see Medicines) (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 838; class IIb).
Not breastfeeding: follow conventional heart failure therapy (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Peripartum cardiomyopathy).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan delivery
actions: If stable, delivery may be delayed to avoid severe prematurity (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).
Without a reversible cause, consider delivery from about 32 weeks, or earlier if medical response is poor (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Delivery in a woman presenting with heart failure).
Avoid ergometrine and carboprost for the third stage (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Delivery).

clinicalManagement.title: Counsel and follow up
actions: Counsel on contraception and future pregnancy; progesterone-based methods do not raise thrombosis risk (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Delivery and Section Peripartum cardiomyopathy).
Book follow-up at 4 to 6 weeks, 3, 6, 12 and 18 months, then yearly for at least 5 years (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Table 2).

regimens.patientGroup: Pregnant or postpartum women with congestion
regimens.dose: 20 to 40 mg intravenously, injected slowly over 1 to 2 minutes; may repeat or raise by 20 mg no sooner than 2 hours after the previous dose (Furosemide label, Section Dosage and Administration).
regimens.frequency: Repeat as needed, then once or twice daily
adjustments: In pregnancy, monitor the foetus because of placental blood flow concerns (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Managing acute heart failure).

monitoring: Urine output, weight, potassium and renal function.

The bromocriptine label warns of stroke, seizures and myocardial infarction with postpartum lactation suppression; weigh this with cardiology. diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Heart failure towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, LVEF below 45%, no other identifiable cause (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Definition and epidemiology, p. 828).
BNP below 100 pg/mL or N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) below 300 pg/mL (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Section Biomarkers, p. 832).
Ejection fraction below 25%, right ventricular involvement, ICU care or cardiogenic shock (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 838).

teaching.scope: Women in late pregnancy or the months after delivery with suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) presenting to the emergency department (ED), obstetric unit or medical ward: recognition, natriuretic peptide, electrocardiogram and echocardiography, acute heart failure care that is safe in pregnancy and lactation, bromocriptine with anticoagulation, delivery planning, referral to an intensive care unit (ICU) or tertiary centre, and follow-up. Uses the Heart Failure Association of the European Society of Cardiology (HFA/ESC) 2019 PPCM position statement and 2021 pregnancy cardiomyopathy statement, and product labels.
learningObjectives: Recognise PPCM from non-specific peripartum symptoms.
Use BNP, ECG and echocardiography to diagnose or exclude it.
Treat acute heart failure with drugs safe in pregnancy.
Pair bromocriptine with anticoagulation and plan follow-up and contraception.
pitfalls: Attributing breathlessness and oedema to normal pregnancy.
Using angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors during pregnancy.
Implanting a defibrillator too early in a patient likely to recover.
keyPoints: LVEF below 45% late in pregnancy or after delivery with no other cause.
BNP below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure unlikely.
About half recover; risk of recurrence depends on recovery.

patientEducation: This is a weakness of the heart muscle linked to pregnancy; many women recover.
Another pregnancy can be dangerous; discuss contraception and plans with your cardiologist (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, p. 840).
Report breathlessness, swelling, palpitations or chest pain at once.
lifestyleAndDiet: Salt and fluid advice from the heart failure team.
mdtReferrals: Cardiologist; obstetrician; anaesthetist; intensivist; neonatologist or paediatrician; cardiac surgeon if mechanical support is needed (HFA/ESC 2021, Section Peripartum cardiomyopathy).
dischargeCriteria: Congestion resolved; heart failure drugs safe for breastfeeding status started; anticoagulation plan clear; contraception and pregnancy counselling given; cardiology follow-up at 4 to 6 weeks booked (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Table 2).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Cardiology review at 4 to 6 weeks, 3, 6, 12 and 18 months, then yearly for at least 5 years with echocardiography; specialist counselling before any future pregnancy (HFA/ESC PPCM 2019, Table 2 and p. 840).
